name: Ganirelix
lead: Ganirelix, sold as Orgalutran and Antagon among other names, is an injectable GnRH antagonist used in assisted reproduction to prevent premature ovulation during ovarian stimulation for IVF [1][2]. It competitively blocks pituitary GnRH receptors, rapidly suppressing LH and FSH, with the effect reversing after stopping [2].

Randomized trials in women undergoing ovarian stimulation compared it with GnRH agonist protocols [3][4][5]. It is a prescription fertility drug; no studies examine it for appearance or muscle outcomes.
infobox: Rx-only in US, EU, Canada, Australia [2]

paras: Its labeled use is inhibiting premature LH surges in women undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation, with ovulation then triggered with hCG [2][5]. Studies have also examined triggering final oocyte maturation with a GnRH agonist after ganirelix cotreatment, including with reference to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome [6][7].

The most common effect is mild redness and sometimes swelling at the injection site; abdominal pain, headache, vaginal bleeding and nausea are also reported, many linked to ovarian hyperstimulation, and anaphylactoid reactions are rare [2]. It is not for use in pregnancy [2].

Ganirelix is a synthetic peptide derived from GnRH with several amino acid substitutions; it binds the receptor more strongly than GnRH itself, and bioavailability is reported at about 91% [2]. Related antagonists such as degarelix have been characterized pharmacologically [8].

A European randomized trial of 730 women found ganirelix with recombinant FSH effective and safe against a buserelin long-protocol reference [3]. Further randomized trials compared it with triptorelin and leuprolide, and a dose-finding study preceded them [4][5][9]. A Cochrane review and a meta-analysis have compared GnRH antagonists with the long agonist protocol [10][11]. A trial of sub-therapeutic GnRH antagonist in lean women with PCOS is registered [12]. All studies concern fertility treatment.

timeline.event: European authorization for Orgalutran; European randomized trial published [2][3].
Cochrane review of GnRH antagonists for assisted conception [10].

card.summary: A GnRH-antagonist fertility drug for IVF; its place on a looks list rests on hormone suppression, not any appearance trial.
card.note: Prescription IVF drug; no appearance or muscle studies.

quick.overview:
Ganirelix is a prescription injection used during IVF to stop the body ovulating too early.

It is well studied in randomized fertility trials, but no study tests it for appearance or muscle goals.
quick.mechanism: It blocks GnRH receptors on the pituitary, quickly lowering LH and FSH; the effect reverses after stopping [2].
quick.risks: Reported effects include injection-site reactions, abdominal pain, headache and nausea; it is not for use in pregnancy, and it is Rx-only [2].
